name: Snake Plant

light.text: Tolerates low light but grows fastest in bright, indirect light. Can handle a few hours of direct sun once acclimated.

water.amount: Soak until water runs from the drainage hole, then empty the saucer.
water.text: Let the soil dry out completely between waterings — about every 2–3 weeks in spring and summer, monthly or less in winter.

humidity.text: Perfectly happy in dry indoor air.

climate: Native to arid West Africa. Grows outdoors year-round in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor; can summer outdoors in shade above 55°F.
soil: Fast-draining cactus/succulent mix in a pot with a drainage hole.
fertilizer: Half-strength balanced fertilizer 2–3 times during spring and summer. None in winter.
propagation: Divide the rhizome when repotting, or root leaf cuttings in water or soil.
problems: Mushy, yellow leaves at the base mean overwatering — the #1 killer.
Wrinkled, curling leaves mean it's finally thirsty.
tip: When in doubt, don't water. A snake plant forgotten for a month is fine; one watered weekly will rot.
why: Thrives on neglect, low light and dry air. Only overwatering hurts it.

name: ZZ Plant

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Even handles offices with only fluorescent light. Avoid harsh direct sun, which scorches leaves.

water.amount: Water thoroughly, then let it drain completely.
water.text: Water when the soil is fully dry, roughly every 2–3 weeks. Its potato-like rhizomes store water for long droughts.

humidity.text: Average or dry household humidity is fine.

climate: Native to dry grasslands of East Africa. Outdoor-hardy only in USDA zones 10–12.
soil: Well-draining potting mix with extra perlite or a cactus mix.
fertilizer: Half-strength houseplant fertilizer once a month in spring and summer.
propagation: Divide the rhizomes, or root individual leaflets in soil (slow — several months).
problems: Yellowing stems usually mean too much water.
Leggy, leaning growth means it wants more light.
tip: Its glossy leaves come naturally; wipe them with a damp cloth instead of using leaf shine.
why: Stores water in its roots and tolerates low light, so it handles weeks of being ignored.

name: Golden Pothos

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Variegation fades in low light; direct afternoon sun burns the leaves.

water.text: Water when the top 1–2 inches of soil are dry, about every 1–2 weeks. Leaves droop visibly when it's thirsty and perk up within hours.

humidity.text: Tolerates normal home humidity; appreciates more but doesn't need it.

climate: Native to the Solomon Islands. Outdoors only in USDA zones 10–12, where it can become invasive.
placement: Indoor; hanging baskets, shelves or trained up a moss pole.
fertilizer: Balanced liquid fertilizer monthly in spring and summer.
propagation: Very easy: root stem cuttings with a node in a glass of water in 2–3 weeks.
problems: Yellow leaves usually mean overwatering.
Long bare vines mean it needs more light or a trim.
tip: Pinch back long vines to make it bushier, then root the cuttings and pot them back in the same pot.
why: Shows you when it's thirsty by drooping, and bounces back from almost anything.

name: Cast Iron Plant

light.text: Low to medium indirect light. One of the best plants for dim corners. Direct sun bleaches and scorches its leaves.

water.amount: Water thoroughly and let excess drain.
water.text: Let the top half of the soil dry out between waterings, roughly every 10–14 days.

climate: Native to forest floors in Japan and Taiwan. Hardy outdoors in USDA zones 7–11 as a shade groundcover.
placement: Indoor, or outdoors in full shade in mild climates.
soil: Regular potting mix with good drainage.
fertilizer: Light feeding monthly in spring and summer only.
propagation: Divide the rhizome clumps in spring.
problems: Brown leaf tips from fluoride in tap water or soggy soil.
Brown scorched patches from direct sun.
tip: It grows slowly, so buy one at the size you want.
why: Earned its name surviving dark, drafty Victorian parlors. Handles cold, shade and missed waterings.

name: Spider Plant

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light. Tolerates lower light but stops producing babies.

water.text: Water when the top inch of soil is dry, roughly weekly in summer. Its thick roots store water if you forget.

humidity.text: Average humidity is fine; very dry air gives brown tips.

climate: Native to southern Africa. Outdoors year-round in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Indoor; outdoors in shade during summer. Great in hanging baskets.
fertilizer: Monthly in spring and summer; overfeeding causes brown tips.
propagation: Pot up the baby 'spiderettes' that dangle from runners — they root in days.
problems: Brown tips from fluoride/chlorine in tap water — try filtered or rainwater.
Pale, washed-out leaves from too much direct sun.
tip: A slightly root-bound spider plant produces more babies, so don't rush to repot.
why: Fast-growing, pet-safe and quick to recover from mistakes.

name: Chinese Evergreen

light.text: Green varieties tolerate low light. Pink and red varieties need medium to bright indirect light to keep their color.

water.amount: Water thoroughly; never leave it standing in water.
water.text: Allow the top 1–2 inches of soil to dry before watering, about every 1–2 weeks.

humidity.text: Average humidity; brown edges in very dry air.

climate: Native to tropical forests of Southeast Asia. Outdoors only in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor. Keep away from cold drafts and AC vents.
fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer every 6–8 weeks in the growing season.
propagation: Division at repotting, or stem cuttings in water.
problems: Cold damage (dark, wet-looking patches) below 55°F.
Yellow lower leaves are normal aging; many at once means overwatering.
tip: Choose a darker green variety for dim rooms and a pink one for bright rooms.
why: Tolerates low light, irregular watering and dry air.

name: Jade Plant

light.text: Needs bright light with at least 4 hours of direct sun daily — a south or west window is ideal.

water.amount: Soak thoroughly, then let it drain completely.
water.text: Water when the soil is completely dry, every 2–3 weeks in summer and about monthly in winter.

climate: Native to South Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
placement: Indoor; loves a summer outdoors in sun (acclimate gradually).
soil: Cactus/succulent mix in a heavy pot (it gets top-heavy).
fertilizer: Diluted succulent fertilizer every 2 months in spring and summer.
propagation: Let a stem or leaf dry for a few days, then set it on dry soil — roots appear in weeks.
problems: Soft, shriveling leaves mean root rot from overwatering.
Stretched, leggy stems mean too little light.
tip: Red-tinged leaf edges are a sign of a happy, sun-fed jade, not a problem.
why: Can go weeks without water and lives for decades, as long as it gets sun.

name: Aloe Vera

light.text: Bright, indirect light or direct morning sun. A sunny windowsill is perfect.

water.amount: Water deeply, then let it drain completely.
water.text: Water when the soil is dry two-thirds of the way down, every 2–3 weeks; even less in winter.

climate: Native to the Arabian Peninsula. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Indoor; can go outside in summer.
soil: Cactus mix in a terracotta pot, which helps soil dry out.
fertilizer: Balanced fertilizer at half strength once or twice a year in spring/summer.
propagation: Separate the offsets (pups) from the base and pot them up.
problems: Brown, mushy leaves from overwatering.
Thin, curled leaves mean it's dehydrated.
Flat, floppy leaves mean too little light.
tip: Snap off a lower leaf for minor burns — the gel inside is soothing.
why: Drought-proof and simple, as long as it has a sunny window.

name: Ponytail Palm

light.text: Bright light with some direct sun. Tolerates medium light but grows slowly there.

water.amount: Water thoroughly, then let it drain completely.
water.text: Its swollen trunk stores water. Let the soil dry completely, about every 2–4 weeks.

climate: Native to semi-desert Mexico — not actually a palm. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–12.
soil: Cactus mix in a shallow, wide pot.
fertilizer: Light feeding 2–3 times in the growing season.
propagation: Separate offsets from the base (rare indoors).
problems: Soft trunk = rot from overwatering.
Brown leaf tips are normal and can be trimmed.
tip: Keep it slightly root-bound; it likes a snug pot.
why: Stores water in its trunk, so it shrugs off long gaps between waterings.

name: Heartleaf Philodendron

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Small leaves and long gaps between them mean it needs more light.

water.text: Water when the top inch or two of soil is dry, about once a week in summer.

humidity.text: Average humidity; grows bigger leaves with more.

climate: Native to Central America and the Caribbean. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor; hanging baskets, shelves, or climbing a pole.
fertilizer: Monthly balanced liquid fertilizer spring through summer.
propagation: Root stem cuttings in water — as easy as pothos.
problems: Yellow leaves from overwatering.
Leggy vines in low light.
tip: Give it something to climb and the leaves get noticeably larger.
why: As forgiving as pothos, with softer heart-shaped leaves.

name: Philodendron Brasil

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light keeps the lime-yellow stripe bright.

water.text: Water when the top inch or two of soil is dry, about weekly.

climate: Cultivar of a Central American vine. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Stem cuttings root easily in water.
problems: Plain green leaves (reversion) in low light — cut those vines back.
Yellowing from soggy soil.
tip: Trim any all-green vines to keep the variegation.
why: Same easygoing nature as heartleaf philodendron, with more color.

name: Corn Plant

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Variegated forms prefer brighter spots.

water.amount: Water thoroughly, preferably with filtered or rain water.
water.text: Let the top 50% of the soil dry before watering, roughly every 10–14 days.

climate: Native to tropical Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
fertilizer: Light monthly feeding in spring and summer.
problems: Brown tips from fluoride in tap water.
Dropping lower leaves is normal as it grows taller.
tip: Cut the cane to any height and it will sprout new heads below the cut.
why: Tolerates low light and irregular care for years.

name: Dragon Tree

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light. Survives lower light but grows thin.

water.text: Let the top half of the soil dry, about every 10–21 days.

humidity.text: Average to dry air is fine.

climate: Native to Madagascar. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
fertilizer: Monthly at half strength in spring and summer.
propagation: Top or cane cuttings in water or soil.
problems: Brown tips from fluoride or dry soil.
Droopy, yellow leaves from overwatering.
tip: Rotate it every few weeks so the canes grow straight.
why: Drought-tolerant, slow-growing and hard to upset.

name: Zebra Haworthia

light.text: Bright indirect light. Unlike most succulents it tolerates medium light; strong sun turns it red or white.

water.text: Water when the soil is completely dry, every 2–3 weeks; monthly in winter.

climate: Native to South Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
fertilizer: Half-strength succulent fertilizer 2–3 times in spring and summer.
problems: Rot from water sitting in the rosette.
Leaves turning white/red from too much sun.
tip: One of the few succulents that stays compact on a desk away from a window.
why: A tiny succulent that tolerates lower light than most and rarely needs water.

name: Lucky Bamboo

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Direct sun scorches it.

water.amount: Keep roots covered with 1–2 inches of water in a vase.
water.text: If grown in water, top up as needed and change the water completely every 1–2 weeks. In soil, keep it lightly moist.

climate: Native to Central Africa (not a true bamboo). Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
soil: None needed — grows in water with pebbles, or in moist potting mix.
fertilizer: A single drop of liquid fertilizer every 2 months when grown in water.
propagation: Cut offshoots and place them in water.
problems: Yellow stalks from chlorine/fluoride or old water.
Green algae in clear vases — use an opaque container.
tip: Use distilled, filtered or rain water to avoid yellow tips.
why: Lives in a vase of water with only an occasional water change.

name: Satin Pothos

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light brings out the silver speckles.

water.text: Wait until the soil is mostly dry. Leaves curl inward when it's thirsty — a handy reminder.

humidity.text: Average humidity; slightly higher keeps leaves flat and glossy.

climate: Native to Southeast Asia. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
placement: Indoor; trailing from shelves or hanging pots.
fertilizer: Monthly at half strength in spring/summer.
propagation: Stem cuttings in water or moss.
problems: Yellow leaves from wet soil.
Crispy edges from very dry air.
tip: Water when the leaves start to curl — it tells you exactly when.
why: Signals thirst clearly and tolerates average homes.

name: Baby Rubber Plant

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light. Variegated forms need the brighter end.

water.amount: Water lightly but thoroughly; drain well.
water.text: Thick leaves store water. Water when the top half of the soil is dry, about every 1–2 weeks.

climate: Native to Florida, Mexico and the Caribbean. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
soil: Airy mix with orchid bark and perlite.
propagation: Stem or leaf cuttings in soil or water.
problems: Wilting with wet soil = root rot.
Leaf drop from cold drafts.
tip: Small root systems prefer a small pot — don't oversize it.
why: Compact, pet-safe and water-storing, so it forgives missed waterings.

name: Yucca Cane

light.text: Bright light with some direct sun.

water.text: Let the soil dry at least halfway, every 2–3 weeks.

climate: Native to Mexico and Central America. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
fertilizer: Two or three light feedings in the growing season.
problems: Soft canes from overwatering.
Brown tips and spots from too much moisture.
tip: Sharp leaf tips — place it out of walkways.
why: Sun-loving and drought-tough, with almost no fuss.

name: Monstera

light.text: Bright indirect light grows the big split leaves. In medium light it survives, but new leaves come in smaller and without holes.

water.text: Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry, about every 1–2 weeks.

humidity.text: Average humidity; 50%+ helps new leaves unfurl cleanly.

climate: Native to Central American rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor; needs floor space and something to climb.
soil: Chunky aroid mix: potting soil, bark and perlite.
fertilizer: Monthly balanced fertilizer in spring and summer.
propagation: Stem cuttings with a node and aerial root, in water or moss.
problems: Yellow lower leaves from overwatering.
No splits (fenestrations) means it wants more light.
tip: Add a moss pole and tuck the aerial roots into it — the leaves grow larger as it climbs.
why: Easy to keep alive, but it needs space, a support and decent light to look its best.

name: Peace Lily

light.text: Low to bright indirect light. Needs medium to bright light to bloom.

water.text: Keep the soil lightly moist; water when the top inch is dry, about weekly. It droops dramatically when thirsty and recovers within hours.

climate: Native to tropical rainforests of the Americas. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
fertilizer: Half-strength monthly in spring and summer.
problems: Brown leaf tips from tap-water minerals or dry air.
No flowers means it needs more light.
tip: Don't wait for the dramatic droop every time — repeated wilting stresses it.
why: Easy and expressive, but it needs regular water and complains loudly if you forget.

name: Rubber Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light. Burgundy and variegated forms need the brightest spot to keep color.

water.text: Water when the top 2 inches are dry, about every 1–2 weeks in summer; less in winter.

climate: Native to Southeast Asia and northeast India. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Air layering or stem cuttings (wear gloves — the white sap irritates skin).
problems: Sudden leaf drop from cold drafts or being moved.
Drooping leaves from under- or overwatering.
tip: Dust the big leaves monthly so they can photosynthesize.
why: Sturdier than other ficus but still drops leaves if moved or chilled.

name: Wax Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light, with some gentle direct morning sun to trigger blooms.

water.text: Thick waxy leaves store water. Let the soil dry almost fully, about every 10–14 days.

climate: Native to eastern Asia and Australia. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
placement: Indoor; hanging baskets or a hoop trellis.
propagation: Stem cuttings in water, moss or soil.
problems: No blooms means too little light or too young.
Mealybugs hiding in leaf joints.
tip: Never cut off old flower stalks (peduncles) — it reblooms from the same spot.
why: Low-maintenance, but blooming needs bright light and patience.

name: Parlor Palm

light.text: Low to medium indirect light. One of the few palms that tolerates dim rooms; direct sun yellows it.

water.amount: Water thoroughly; don't let it sit in water.
water.text: Water when the top inch of soil is dry, about weekly.

humidity.text: Average humidity; very dry air invites spider mites.

climate: Native to rainforests of Mexico and Guatemala. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
fertilizer: Light feeding 2–3 times in spring and summer.
propagation: Seed only — the clumps are many seedlings and dividing is risky.
problems: Brown tips from dry air or salt buildup.
Spider mites in dry heated rooms.
tip: Rinse it in the shower every couple of months to keep spider mites away.
why: Low-light-friendly and pet-safe, but needs steady watering and some humidity.

name: Dumb Cane

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.text: Water when the top inch or two is dry, about weekly.

climate: Native to Central and South America. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Cane sections laid on moist soil, or top cuttings.
problems: Lower leaves yellowing and dropping (natural, or overwatering).
Leaning toward the window — rotate it weekly.
tip: Very toxic sap — keep away from kids and pets and wash hands after pruning.
why: Grows easily, but needs regular water, decent light and careful placement because it's toxic.

name: Arrowhead Plant

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light. Pink varieties need bright light.

water.text: Keep soil lightly moist; water when the top inch is dry, about weekly.

climate: Native to Latin American rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Stem cuttings root fast in water.
problems: Droops quickly when dry.
Brown crispy edges in dry air.
tip: Prune regularly to keep it bushy; unpruned it starts to climb.
why: Easy to grow but thirstier than pothos.

name: Swiss Cheese Vine

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Water when the top inch is dry, about weekly. Doesn't like drying out completely.

climate: Native to Central and South America. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Crispy leaves from dry air.
Yellowing from soggy soil.
tip: Hang it near a bright window and let it cascade.
why: Fast and fun, but it wants more humidity and consistent moisture than pothos.

name: Mini Monstera

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Water when the top 1–2 inches are dry, about weekly.

climate: Native to Thailand and Malaysia. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor; give it a pole to climb.
problems: Yellow leaves from overwatering.
Small unsplit leaves in low light.
tip: Grows feet per year in good light — prune to keep it compact.
why: Vigorous and tolerant, but needs good light and a support.

name: Wandering Dude

light.text: Bright indirect light keeps the purple and silver stripes vivid.

water.text: Keep evenly moist; water when the top inch is dry.

climate: Native to Mexico and Central America. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–12 (spreads quickly).
placement: Indoor hanging basket; outdoor annual in summer.
propagation: Cuttings root in water within a week.
problems: Leggy with bare stems — pinch back regularly.
Faded color in low light.
tip: Restart it from cuttings every year or two to keep it full.
why: Nearly impossible to kill, but it gets leggy without regular pinching.

name: String of Hearts

light.text: Bright indirect light with some direct sun.

water.text: Let the soil dry almost completely, about every 10–14 days.

climate: Native to southern Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
placement: Indoor hanging pot in a sunny window.
propagation: Lay vines on soil or root the little tubers that form along the stems.
problems: Sparse leaves and long gaps in low light.
Shriveled vines from root rot.
tip: Leaves feel soft and thin when it's thirsty.
why: Forgiving with water, but needs a bright window.

name: Burro's Tail

light.text: Bright light with several hours of direct sun.

water.text: Water when fully dry, every 2–3 weeks.

climate: Native to Mexico. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
placement: Indoor hanging pot; patio in summer.
fertilizer: Half-strength 2–3 times in the growing season.
propagation: Fallen leaves root on dry soil.
problems: Leaves drop at a touch — hang it where it won't be bumped.
Pale, stretched stems from too little sun.
tip: Pick a spot and leave it there; moving it costs leaves.
why: Easy watering, but it needs sun and doesn't like being handled.

name: Watermelon Peperomia

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.text: Water when the top half of the soil is dry.

climate: Native to South America. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
soil: Airy mix with perlite and bark.
propagation: Leaf cuttings — even half a leaf will root.
problems: Stems collapse from overwatering.
Curling leaves when dry.
tip: Keep it in a snug pot; peperomias have tiny roots.
why: Small and pet-safe, but more sensitive to overwatering than baby rubber plant.

name: Chinese Money Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light. Rotate weekly — it leans hard toward the window.

water.text: Water when the top inch or two is dry; leaves droop when thirsty.

climate: Native to Yunnan, China. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
propagation: Pot up the babies that pop up from the soil — perfect for sharing.
problems: Cupped/domed leaves from too much or too little light.
Brown spots from overwatering.
tip: Known as the 'friendship plant' because it's so easy to share pups.
why: Easy, but needs bright light and rotating to stay symmetrical.

name: Bromeliad

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.amount: Keep the central cup ¼ full; water the soil lightly.
water.text: Refresh the water in the central cup weekly and let the soil dry between light waterings.

climate: Native to tropical Americas, grows on trees. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
fertilizer: Quarter-strength fertilizer into the cup monthly in summer.
propagation: Each plant blooms once then produces pups; pot them when they're a third the parent's size.
problems: Rot from stagnant cup water — flush it weekly.
Mother plant dying after bloom is natural.
tip: The colorful bract lasts for months; enjoy it, then grow the pups.
why: Undemanding, but has an unusual watering routine and a single bloom cycle.

name: Air Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light; a bathroom window is perfect.

water.amount: Soak in room-temperature water for 20–30 minutes.
water.text: Soak weekly, then shake and dry upside down for a few hours so water doesn't sit in the base.

humidity.text: Loves humid rooms; mist between soaks if air is dry.

climate: Native to the Americas, growing on trees and rocks. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Indoor; no pot or soil needed.
soil: None — display on wood, wire or shells.
fertilizer: Bromeliad fertilizer in the soak water once a month.
problems: Rotting base from not drying after soaking.
Curled, crispy leaves from dehydration.
tip: Never put it in a closed terrarium — it needs airflow to dry.
why: No soil, but needs a weekly soak-and-dry routine.

name: Money Tree

light.text: Bright indirect light; tolerates medium.

water.text: Water when the top 2–4 inches are dry, about every 1–2 weeks.

climate: Native to Central and South American wetlands. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
soil: Peat-based mix with sand or perlite.
problems: Leaf drop after moving or from drafts.
Yellowing from soggy roots in decorative pots without drainage.
tip: Rotate a quarter turn each time you water to keep the braid even.
why: Pet-safe and tolerant, though it sulks when moved.

name: Kentia Palm

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light; tolerates lower light than most palms.

water.text: Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry.

climate: Native to Lord Howe Island, Australia. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
fertilizer: Palm fertilizer 2–3 times in the growing season.
problems: Brown tips from dry air or salts.
Spider mites.
tip: The most elegant low-light-tolerant palm — worth the price for a big pet-safe statement.
why: The toughest palm for indoors, but slow and pricey to replace.

name: Umbrella Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Let the top half of the soil dry between waterings.

climate: Native to Taiwan and Hainan. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Leaf drop from overwatering or cold.
Spider mites and scale.
tip: Prune the top to encourage a fuller shape.
why: Robust and fast-recovering, but prone to pests.

name: Ficus Ginseng

light.text: Bright light with some direct morning sun.

water.text: Water when the top inch of soil is dry; don't let it fully dry out.

climate: Native to Southeast Asia. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
fertilizer: Every 2 weeks at half strength in the growing season.
problems: Leaf drop after moves or drafts.
Scale insects.
tip: The easiest 'bonsai' for beginners — trim new shoots back to 2–3 leaves.
why: A forgiving starter bonsai that still needs good light and steady watering.

name: Christmas Cactus

light.text: Bright indirect light; harsh sun reddens the segments.

water.text: Water when the top inch is dry. Unlike desert cacti, it doesn't want to dry out completely.

climate: A rainforest cactus native to Brazil. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
fertilizer: Monthly from spring to late summer; stop in fall.
propagation: Twist off 2–3 segment pieces and root them in soil.
problems: Bud drop from moving or temperature swings.
No blooms without a fall cool/dark period.
tip: To get blooms, give it 12+ hours of darkness and cooler nights (50–60°F) for 6 weeks in fall.
why: Easy most of the year, but blooming takes a little seasonal planning.

name: Echeveria

light.text: Full direct sun — at least 6 hours. Indoors it needs your sunniest window or a grow light.

water.amount: Soak the soil (not the rosette) and drain.
water.text: Water only when the soil is bone dry.

climate: Native to semi-desert Mexico and Central America. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Sunny windowsill, or outdoors in warm months.
fertilizer: Diluted succulent fertilizer once or twice in summer.
problems: Stretching ('etiolation') toward light.
Rot from water in the rosette.
tip: If it's stretching, it needs more sun, not more water.
why: Barely needs water, but most homes don't have enough sun for it.

name: Kalanchoe

light.text: Bright light with some direct sun.

water.text: Let the soil dry out between waterings.

climate: Native to Madagascar. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
fertilizer: Monthly during growth; stop when budding.
problems: Rot from overwatering.
Won't rebloom without short days.
tip: Reblooms after about 6 weeks of 14-hour nights in fall.
why: Easy succulent care, plus a rebloom trick if you want flowers again.

name: Pincushion Cactus

light.text: Full sun — 4–6+ hours direct light.

water.text: Water only when bone dry; barely at all in winter.

climate: Native to Mexico and the southwestern US. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
fertilizer: Cactus fertilizer once or twice in summer.
problems: Rot from wet soil, especially in winter.
Lopsided growth toward the light.
tip: A cool, dry winter rest triggers its ring of spring flowers.
why: Almost no watering, but it needs real sun.

name: Purple Shamrock

light.text: Bright indirect light. Leaves open by day and fold at night.

water.text: Water when the top inch is dry.

climate: Native to Brazil. Outdoors in USDA zones 8–11.
problems: Goes dormant and dies back — it's resting, not dead.
Leggy in low light.
tip: If it collapses, stop watering for a few weeks; it regrows from the bulbs.
why: Easy, but its dormancy surprises new owners.

name: Mint

light.text: Bright light with 4+ hours of sun; a south window or grow light indoors.

water.text: Keep soil consistently moist — water when the surface feels dry.

climate: Native to Europe and Asia. Perennial outdoors in USDA zones 3–9.
placement: Indoor or outdoor in containers (it spreads aggressively in beds).
propagation: Cuttings root in water within days.
problems: Wilts fast when dry.
Leggy indoors without enough light.
tip: Harvest often — cutting stems keeps it bushy and tasty.
why: Vigorous, but thirsty and light-hungry indoors.

name: Prayer Plant

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light. Direct sun fades the patterns.

water.amount: Water with room-temp, filtered water until it drains.
water.text: Keep soil evenly moist but never soggy; water when the top half-inch is dry.

humidity.text: Needs 50–60%+. Use a humidifier or pebble tray.

climate: Native to Brazilian rainforest floors. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
placement: Indoor; bathrooms with a window are ideal.
propagation: Stem cuttings below a node, or division.
problems: Crispy brown edges from dry air or tap water.
Curling leaves from underwatering.
tip: Its leaves fold up at night like hands in prayer — that's normal.
why: Needs consistent moisture, humidity and filtered water.

name: Boston Fern

light.text: Bright, indirect light. No direct sun.

water.amount: Water thoroughly so the whole root ball is moist.
water.text: Keep soil consistently damp — check every couple of days.

humidity.text: Needs high humidity (60%+); mist daily or use a humidifier.

climate: Native to humid tropical regions. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Indoor or shaded porch hanging basket.
problems: Shedding, crispy fronds from dry air — the most common issue.
Yellowing from soggy soil.
tip: Move it to a shady porch in summer; it thrives outdoors in humid weather.
why: Sheds constantly in dry homes; needs frequent water and humidity.

name: Bird's Nest Fern

light.text: Medium indirect light.

water.amount: Water the soil around the base, not into the center rosette.
water.text: Keep soil lightly moist.

climate: Native to tropical Asia, Australia and East Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Rotting center from water pooling in the nest.
Brown edges in dry air.
tip: Don't touch the delicate new fronds as they unfurl from the center.
why: Easier than most ferns but still needs humidity and careful watering.

name: Staghorn Fern

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.amount: Soak the mount or root ball for 10–20 minutes.
water.text: Soak weekly in summer, every 2–3 weeks in winter; mist in between.

climate: Native to Australian and Javan forests, growing on trees. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–12.
placement: Mounted on a wall board indoors, or shaded patio.
problems: Browning shield fronds at the base are normal — don't remove them.
Rot from constant wetness.
tip: Displayed mounted on a board, it looks like living wall art.
why: A soak-and-mist routine plus high humidity.

name: English Ivy

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Keep slightly moist; water when the surface is dry.

humidity.text: Prefers cool, humid air — struggles in hot, dry rooms.

climate: Native to Europe and western Asia. Hardy outdoors in USDA zones 4–9 (invasive in many areas).
placement: Indoor in cool rooms. Avoid planting outdoors where it's invasive.
problems: Spider mites in warm, dry rooms — the main issue.
Brown, crispy edges in dry heat.
tip: Shower it monthly to keep spider mites off.
why: Easy outdoors, but indoors it fights spider mites and dry heat.

name: String of Pearls

light.text: Bright light with a few hours of gentle direct sun.

water.amount: Water thoroughly but sparingly; drain well.
water.text: Water when the top half-inch is dry; pearls shrivel when thirsty.

climate: Native to southwest Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–12.
placement: Hanging pot in a bright window.
soil: Gritty cactus mix in a shallow terracotta pot.
propagation: Lay strand cuttings on dry soil.
problems: Root rot and dying crown from overwatering — very common.
Bare top from too little light.
tip: Hang it so the crown gets light, not just the strands.
why: Its shallow roots rot easily, so the watering balance is tight.

name: Polka Dot Begonia

light.text: Bright indirect light; no direct sun.

water.amount: Water at soil level; avoid wetting leaves.
water.text: Water when the top inch is dry. Wilts if too dry, rots if too wet.

humidity.text: Prefers 50%+ but don't mist (causes leaf spots).

climate: Native to Brazil. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Powdery mildew in stagnant air.
Leaf drop from wet or cold roots.
tip: Pinch tips regularly to keep it bushy instead of tall and cane-like.
why: Needs humidity without wet leaves and a careful watering balance.

name: Rex Begonia

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.amount: Water at the soil, not the leaves.
water.text: Let the top inch dry, then water.

climate: Hybrids of Asian forest begonias. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Leaf cuttings — cut the veins and pin the leaf to soil.
problems: Powdery mildew.
Rot from overwatering, especially in winter.
tip: It may go semi-dormant in winter; water less then.
why: Gorgeous but sensitive to watering, humidity and mildew.

name: African Violet

light.text: Bright indirect light, 10–14 hours a day. Thrives under grow lights.

water.amount: Water from the bottom with room-temperature water.
water.text: Keep slightly moist. Cold water or water on leaves leaves spots.

climate: Native to Tanzanian mountain forests. Indoor plant everywhere.
soil: African violet mix (light and slightly acidic).
fertilizer: African violet fertilizer at quarter strength with every watering.
propagation: Leaf cuttings in soil or water.
problems: No blooms means not enough light.
Crown rot from wet soil.
tip: Self-watering violet pots make it much easier.
why: Needs specific watering technique and lots of light to keep blooming.

name: Moth Orchid

light.text: Bright indirect light, such as an east window. Direct midday sun burns leaves.

water.amount: Soak the bark for 10 minutes, then drain completely.
water.text: Water when roots turn silvery and the bark is nearly dry, about weekly. (Ice cubes are a crutch, not ideal.)

climate: Native to Southeast Asian tropics, growing on trees. Indoor plant in most zones.
soil: Orchid bark or sphagnum moss — never regular soil.
fertilizer: Weak orchid fertilizer ('weekly, weakly') during growth.
problems: Mushy brown roots from overwatering.
No reblooming without a cooler fall (55–65°F nights).
tip: After blooms fade, cut the spike above a node — it may rebloom.
why: Simple once you learn its rhythm, but very different from regular houseplants.

name: Anthurium

light.text: Bright indirect light. Low light means no blooms.

water.text: Let the top inch dry, then water.

climate: Native to Colombian and Ecuadorian rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
fertilizer: Phosphorus-rich fertilizer at quarter strength every 2 weeks.
propagation: Division or stem cuttings with aerial roots.
problems: Yellow leaves from overwatering.
Brown tips from dry air.
tip: Each 'flower' (a waxy spathe) can last 2–3 months.
why: Blooming needs high humidity, bright light and steady care.

name: Weeping Fig

light.text: Bright indirect light, ideally near a large window.

water.text: Water when the top inch is dry; keep consistent.

climate: Native to Southeast Asia and Australia. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Dramatic leaf drop when moved, chilled or over/under-watered.
Scale and mealybugs.
tip: Pick its spot and don't move it — it often drops leaves after any change.
why: Sensitive to every change in light, temperature or watering.

name: Bird of Paradise

light.text: Very bright light with several hours of direct sun.

water.text: Water when the top 2–3 inches are dry.

climate: Native to South Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor next to your sunniest window; patio in summer.
problems: Split leaves are natural (wind adaptation).
Brown, curling leaves from underwatering or low humidity.
tip: Rarely blooms indoors — grow it for the huge banana-like leaves.
why: Needs lots of light and space; drama-free otherwise.

name: Areca Palm

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Keep the soil lightly moist; water when the top inch dries.

climate: Native to Madagascar. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Brown tips from fluoride and dry air.
Spider mites.
tip: Use distilled or rain water — areca palms are very sensitive to tap-water salts.
why: Pet-safe and lush, but sensitive to water quality and dry air.

name: Majesty Palm

light.text: Very bright light with some direct sun.

water.text: Keep evenly moist — it's a riverbank palm and hates drying out.

climate: Native to riverbanks in Madagascar. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
placement: Indoor in a very bright room; thrives outdoors in summer.
problems: Yellowing from too little light (very common indoors).
Spider mites.
tip: Cheap at big-box stores but often declines indoors — give it your brightest spot.
why: Thirsty, light-hungry and humidity-dependent.

name: Croton

light.text: Bright light with some direct sun to keep the colors vivid.

water.text: Keep slightly moist; water when the top inch dries.

climate: Native to Indonesia and the western Pacific. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Leaf drop when first brought home or moved.
Spider mites; dull green leaves in low light.
tip: Expect it to sulk and drop leaves for a few weeks after you bring it home.
why: Needs strong light and humidity and reacts badly to change.

name: Nerve Plant

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.text: Keep soil evenly moist. It faints dramatically when dry and revives after watering.

climate: Native to Peruvian rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
problems: Collapses when dry.
Crispy leaves in dry air.
tip: Put it in a closed terrarium and it nearly takes care of itself.
why: Needs constant moisture and humidity — or a terrarium.

name: Polka Dot Plant

light.text: Bright indirect light keeps the spots colorful.

water.text: Keep soil lightly moist.

climate: Native to Madagascar. Grown as an annual outdoors; perennial in USDA zones 10–11.
problems: Gets leggy quickly — pinch often.
Wilts fast when dry.
tip: Pinch off flower spikes; flowering signals the end of its life cycle.
why: Short-lived and leggy without frequent pinching and watering.

name: Asparagus Fern

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Keep slightly moist; tuberous roots store some water.

climate: Native to southern Africa (not a true fern). Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
problems: Shedding needles in dry air.
Yellowing in too much sun.
tip: Watch for small thorns on the stems when pruning.
why: Sheds heavily in dry homes.

name: Cyclamen

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.amount: Water from the bottom; keep water off the tuber.
water.text: Keep moist while blooming; nearly stop watering when it goes dormant in summer.

climate: Native to the Mediterranean. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
problems: Collapse in warm rooms.
Tuber rot from overhead watering.
tip: A cool windowsill (50–65°F) keeps it blooming for months.
why: Needs cool temperatures, bottom watering and a summer dormancy.

name: Poinsettia

light.text: Bright light, 6+ hours.

water.amount: Water thoroughly and discard drainage (remove foil wrappers).
water.text: Water when the top inch is dry.

climate: Native to Mexico. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
fertilizer: Monthly after blooming, spring to fall.
problems: Leaf drop from cold drafts.
Won't recolor without strict long nights.
tip: Needs 14 hours of total darkness nightly from October to recolor its bracts.
why: Easy for the holidays, demanding to keep and rebloom.

name: Basil

light.text: 6–8 hours of direct sun, or a grow light. Indoor windows are often too dim.

water.amount: Water at the soil level until it drains.
water.text: Keep evenly moist; it wilts fast when dry.

climate: Native to tropical Asia. A warm-season annual outdoors everywhere.
placement: Sunny windowsill or outdoors in summer.
propagation: Cuttings root in water in a week.
problems: Leggy and weak in low light.
Flowering ends leaf production — pinch flower buds.
tip: Harvest from the top, just above a leaf pair, to make it branch.
why: Needs strong sun, frequent watering and regular harvesting.

name: Calathea
botanical: Goeppertia spp. (e.g. G. orbifolia, G. lancifolia)

light.text: Medium indirect light. Direct sun fades and burns the patterns.

water.amount: Water with distilled, filtered or rain water until it drains.
water.text: Keep evenly moist — never soggy, never dry. Tap water causes brown edges.

humidity.text: Needs 60%+ humidity; a humidifier is practically required.

climate: Native to tropical American rainforest understory. Outdoors in USDA zones 11–12.
placement: Indoor, away from vents and drafts.
problems: Crispy brown edges — dry air or tap water.
Curling leaves from underwatering.
Spider mites.
tip: Group it with other plants and a humidifier — it's happiest in a humid little jungle.
why: Fussy about humidity, water quality and consistency; shows every mistake.

name: Fiddle Leaf Fig

light.text: Very bright light directly beside a large window; some direct morning sun is ideal.

water.amount: Water deeply until it drains, then let excess drain fully.
water.text: Water when the top 2 inches are dry. Be consistent — irregular watering causes brown spots and drop.

climate: Native to West African rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor, permanently in the brightest spot you have.
soil: Well-draining mix with bark and perlite.
problems: Brown spots from root rot (overwatering).
Leaf drop from moves, drafts or low light.
tip: Don't move it once it's settled. Rotate a quarter turn every few weeks instead.
why: Hates change, needs very bright light and drops leaves dramatically when unhappy.

name: Maidenhair Fern

light.text: Medium indirect light; no direct sun.

water.text: Never let it dry out — even one dry day can crisp the fronds. Check daily.

humidity.text: Needs 70%+ humidity; terrarium or humidifier recommended.

climate: Native to tropical Americas. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–11.
problems: Entire fronds crisp up from a single dry spell.
Browning in dry heated air.
tip: If it crisps, cut it back to the soil and keep it moist — it often regrows.
why: Needs daily attention to moisture and very high humidity.

name: Alocasia

light.text: Bright indirect light.

water.text: Keep lightly moist in growth; let the top inch dry. Water much less in winter.

climate: Hybrid of Southeast Asian species. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
propagation: Separate the corms (bulbs) in the soil.
problems: Spider mites — the #1 issue.
Winter dormancy where leaves drop (not dead!).
tip: Check leaf undersides weekly for spider mites.
why: Prone to spider mites, dormancy and root rot; needs humidity.

name: Stromanthe Triostar

light.text: Bright indirect light for the pink color.

water.text: Keep evenly moist.

climate: Native to Brazilian rainforests. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Crispy edges.
Faded color in low light.
tip: Treat it like a calathea that needs more light.
why: As fussy as calathea about humidity and water.

name: Venus Flytrap

light.text: Full direct sun, 6+ hours, or a strong grow light.

water.amount: Stand the pot in a tray of distilled or rain water.
water.text: Keep constantly wet with mineral-free water only — tap water kills it.

climate: Native only to bogs of North and South Carolina. Outdoors in USDA zones 7–10.
placement: Best outdoors in sun; needs a cold winter dormancy (35–50°F) for 3 months.
soil: Peat moss and perlite — never fertilized potting soil.
problems: Dies without winter dormancy.
Blackening from tap water or fertilizer.
tip: Don't trigger the traps for fun — each one only closes a handful of times.
why: Needs pure water, full sun and a cold dormancy every winter.

name: Gardenia

light.text: Bright light with some direct sun.

water.amount: Water with room-temperature rain or distilled water.
water.text: Keep evenly moist but not soggy.

climate: Native to southern China and Japan. Outdoors in USDA zones 8–11.
placement: Best outdoors in warm climates; tricky indoors.
fertilizer: Acid-loving plant fertilizer every 2–4 weeks in growth.
problems: Bud drop from temperature swings or dry air.
Yellow leaves from alkaline water/soil.
tip: Nights around 60–65°F are needed for buds to set.
why: Needs acidic soil, high humidity and precise temperatures to flower.

name: Meyer Lemon Tree

light.text: 8+ hours of direct sun, or a strong grow light in winter.

water.text: Water when the top 2 inches are dry.

climate: Hybrid from China. Outdoors in USDA zones 9–11.
placement: Outdoors in summer, indoors by your sunniest window in winter.
fertilizer: Citrus fertilizer every 4–6 weeks in growth.
problems: Leaf drop when moved indoors in fall.
Scale and spider mites.
tip: Hand-pollinate indoor flowers with a small paintbrush to get fruit.
why: Needs intense light, seasonal moves and pest vigilance to fruit.

name: Rosemary

light.text: 6–8 hours of direct sun; indoors needs a grow light.

water.text: Let the top inch dry, but don't let it dry completely — dead roots don't show until it's too late.

climate: Native to the Mediterranean. Perennial outdoors in USDA zones 7–10.
placement: Outdoors in sun; indoors over winter with lots of light.
problems: Powdery mildew indoors.
Sudden death from root rot or a single drought.
tip: Run a small fan nearby indoors to prevent mildew.
why: Needs sun and airflow most homes lack, and dies with little warning.

name: Lavender

light.text: Full sun, 8+ hours. Indoors only with a powerful grow light.

water.text: Let the soil dry out between waterings.

climate: Native to the Mediterranean. Perennial outdoors in USDA zones 5–9.
placement: Outdoors. Very difficult as a long-term houseplant.
problems: Root rot from wet soil.
Weak, floppy growth indoors.
tip: Best kept on a sunny patio; bring in only for short visits.
why: Needs far more sun than a home can usually provide.

name: Peperomia Hope

light.text: Medium to bright indirect light.

water.text: Round, succulent-like leaves store water; let the soil dry out mostly.

climate: Hybrid of South American species. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
placement: Indoor shelf or small hanging pot.
fertilizer: Half-strength a few times in growth.
problems: Rot from overwatering.
Leaf drop from cold.
tip: A perfect trailing plant for pet owners.
why: Small, pet-safe and drought-tolerant.

name: Janet Craig Dracaena

light.text: Low to medium indirect light — one of the best for dim rooms.

water.amount: Water thoroughly with filtered water and drain.
water.text: Let the top half of the soil dry.

climate: Native to tropical Africa. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Brown tips from fluoride.
tip: Its deep green leaves handle offices and dim hallways.
why: A tough, low-light plant with almost no needs.

name: Cylindrical Snake Plant

light.text: Low to bright light; best in bright indirect.

water.text: Water only when fully dry, every 3–4 weeks.

climate: Native to Angola. Outdoors in USDA zones 10–12.
problems: Rot from overwatering.
tip: Sculptural and narrow — fits windowsills and tight corners.
why: Even more drought-tolerant than the classic snake plant.
